column6: The commentary treats Abraham's and Moses' first pages as a durable warning; Deuteronomy puts Moses' written Torah beside the ark as a witness against Israel, making the old text itself testimony.
Moses is told to write a song and put it in Israel's mouths as a witness; this joins the commentary's two preservations, written pages and words retained by recitation.
Isaiah is commanded to inscribe a warning in a book for future days as a lasting witness, closely matching the commentary's old pages whose warning remains present.
The commentary places the dried pasture beside pages that have not vanished; Isaiah contrasts withering grass and fading flower with God's word standing forever.
Jehoiakim cuts and burns Jeremiah's written scroll, giving a concrete instance of the commentary's point that a page can be damaged or suppressed by human hands.
After the king burns the scroll, Jeremiah is told to write its words again; the message outlasts a vulnerable sheet, paralleling the commentary's contrast between fragile writing and enduring speech.

column5: book of remembrance and the divine name
column6: Malachi says a book of remembrance is written for those who fear the Lord and esteem his name; this links the commentary's fear, remembrance, prayerful naming, and preserved record.
The commentary distinguishes loose sheets from a single bound book; Exodus gives Moses tablets of stone with instruction written by God, a distinct durable written form associated with him.
Moses commands that his words remain on Israel's heart, a direct scriptural counterpart to the commentary's word preserved in an instructed memory as well as on pages.
The same instruction is to be written on house doorposts and gates; the verse supplies a concrete domestic written counterpart to words held in the heart.
Habakkuk is told to write the vision on tablets plainly so a reader can run with it; this joins the commentary's open writing surface to public reading and transmission.

column5: reading and explanation of the book
column6: The law is read from the book and interpreted so the hearers understand; this illuminates the commentary's messenger who voices written pages rather than relying on silent inspection alone.

column5: one person's guilt is not another's
column6: The law forbids putting children to death for parents' crimes; it gives a legal form of the first rule quoted from Abraham's pages, that no bearer carries another's burden.

column5: the sinner bears his own guilt
column6: Ezekiel says the child does not bear a parent's guilt and the person who sins bears that person's own consequence; this develops the commentary's individual-accountability reading of the old pages.

column5: each dies for their own sin
column6: Jeremiah answers the inherited sour-grapes proverb by saying each person dies for their own sin, a direct correction of the idea that one generation bears another's guilt.
Daniel's heavenly court opens books before the judge; this is a close Jewish-scriptural counterpart to the commentary's pages opened at the end and deeds brought into judgment.

column5: opened books and judgment by deeds
column6: Revelation depicts books opened and the dead judged from what is written in them according to their deeds; it brings the commentary's opened pages and individual recompense together.

column5: writing on hearts rather than stone
column6: Paul calls the Corinthians a letter written by the Spirit on human hearts, explicitly contrasting stone tablets and inward inscription; this gives a Christian reading of the commentary's two ways of keeping one word.

column5: law written in minds and hearts
column6: Hebrews applies Jeremiah's new-covenant promise of law written inwardly; it interprets Moses' external written instruction through the inward preservation that the commentary sets beside pages.
The Qur'anic Moses is summoned in a sacred valley before being sent to Pharaoh; Exodus also marks Moses' call by holy ground, while its burning-bush scene gives the encounter a different sign.
The commentary reads Moses' warning to Pharaoh as a model for the surah's admonition; Exodus likewise makes the encounter with Pharaoh the commission's stated purpose.

column5: Pharaoh asks who the Lord is
column6: Exodus has Pharaoh ask who YHWH is and deny that he will heed him, whereas the commentary's Qur'anic Pharaoh claims the highest lordship for himself; the shared confrontation highlights different forms of defiance.

Exodus' magicians reproduce Aaron's sign at first, while the commentary's Qur'anic magicians end by confessing faith after Moses' sign prevails; the same contest receives a sharply different human outcome.

When unable to reproduce the plague, Pharaoh's magicians say it is God's finger, but the scene does not show them converting; the Qur'anic magicians' explicit submission makes that difference significant.

column5: Abraham leaves his land and father's house
column6: The commentary praises the first-pages figure who left the inherited path; Genesis begins Abraham's call by commanding him to leave country, kin, and father's house, though it does not itself mention idol-breaking.

Genesis says Abraham obeyed God's voice and kept commandments, statutes, and teachings; it presents Abraham as already faithful to instruction before Moses, supporting the commentary's pairing of their earlier pages.
The midrash expands Abraham's rejection of ancestral worship into the story of breaking the idols in Terah's shop; it makes explicit the departure from inherited custom that the commentary stresses.

Jubilees has Abram challenge his father over the idols and their worship; this Second Temple retelling supplies the explicit anti-idolatry background behind the commentary's contrast between Abraham and his ancestors.
Stephen retells Abraham's call as occurring in Mesopotamia before he settled in Haran; the Christian retelling emphasizes that the patriarch's path begins by leaving his natal setting.
Hebrews says Abraham obeyed the call and went out without knowing his destination; its interpretation makes the departure from inherited security an act of trust in God's guidance.

column5: ancestry does not guarantee Abraham's way
column6: John the Baptist rejects reliance on having Abraham as father and says God can raise children from stones; this directly supports the commentary's claim that old ancestry alone is no measure of truth.

column5: Abraham's children must do Abraham's works
column6: Jesus answers a claim of descent by requiring Abraham's works; it sharpens the commentary's contrast between honoring the ancient patriarch and simply repeating ancestral custom.

column5: Moses and the prophets are to be heard
column6: In the parable Abraham says the brothers have Moses and the prophets and should listen to them; the old written testimony is presented as sufficient warning to people who turn away.

column5: a risen messenger cannot force belief
column6: Abraham says those who refuse Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by someone rising from the dead; this intensifies the commentary's claim that the old pages already confront the rejecter.
Jesus says Moses wrote about him; this Christian reading makes Moses' written testimony a witness to a later messenger, like the commentary's old pages bearing a warning read anew.
Jesus asks how hearers will believe his words if they do not believe Moses' writings; the verse directly stages the commentary's contrast between written warning and refusal to hear it.
Jesus receives and opens Isaiah's scroll in the synagogue; the scene gives a concrete Christian instance of a messenger voicing an old written page to a present audience.

column5: Moses chooses affliction over passing pleasure
column6: Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God's people rather than temporary enjoyment in Pharaoh's house; it concretely parallels the commentary's preference for the lasting afterlife over worldly life.

column5: Moses values future reward above Egypt's riches
column6: Hebrews says Moses counted reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looked to the reward; this interprets the same choice of lasting good over present advantage that the commentary sees in Moses' magicians.
Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where decay and theft cannot destroy it; this gives a direct ethical counterpart to preferring the more enduring hereafter over worldly life.
John contrasts the passing world and its desire with the one who does God's will abiding forever; this closely matches the commentary's contrast between the transient present and what lasts.

column5: judgment according to each person's deeds
column6: Paul says God repays each according to works; this Christian formulation joins the commentary's reading of the pages' rule that each person's striving is seen and fully requited.

column5: each receives wages for own labor
column6: Paul says each worker receives wages according to that worker's labor; this is a close match for the pages' claim that a person has only what they strive for and receives recompense.
Paul says each will carry their own load, a concise Christian counterpart to the commentary's first rule that no bearer takes another's burden.

column5: visible things are temporary, unseen things eternal
column6: Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal; it gives a Christian formulation of the commentary's choice between the fading present and lasting hereafter.

column5: flesh is like grass that withers
column6: Peter quotes the grass and flower that fade, matching the commentary's pasture that dries and is swept away while the word remains.
Peter applies Isaiah's enduring word to the proclaimed gospel; this adds a Christian reading of the old word as surviving through present recitation.

Mark applies Isaiah's undying worm and unquenched fire to Gehenna; Isaiah speaks of corpses and worms, while Mark makes the image an eschatological warning, a useful contrast to the Qur'anic person who neither dies nor lives.
Isaiah describes corpses of rebels exposed to worms and fire, not a person who neither dies nor lives; the shared fire image clarifies the distinct afterlife claim made in the commentary.
Isaiah pictures the host of heaven falling as the sky rolls up like a scroll; this is the opposite cosmic motion to the pages spread open in the commentary's cited end-time scene.

column5: sky withdrawn like a rolled scroll
column6: Revelation says the sky vanished like a scroll being rolled up; alongside the commentary's opened pages, it supplies the paired image of cosmic writing rolled shut.
Exodus says God hardens Pharaoh's heart during the signs, adding divine hardening to the refusal that the commentary frames as Pharaoh's boast, denial, and turning away.

The commentary contrasts an old warning with mere appeal to ancestors; Ezekiel tells the next generation not to follow their fathers' statutes or defile themselves with idols, making the break with inherited practice explicit.
God says Abraham will command his children and household to keep the Lord's way by doing righteousness and justice; this makes his continuing legacy an ethical warning handed to later generations.

column5: stars as a promise of descendants
column6: Genesis uses the night sky's stars to promise Abraham innumerable descendants, whereas the commentary's Abraham rejects celestial bodies that set; the shared star scene distinguishes a sign of promise from an object of worship.

The midrash reads God's taking Abraham outside to see the stars as release from astrological destiny; it adds a Jewish interpretation to the commentary's scene where Abraham watches heavenly bodies set and seeks God's guidance.

The Talmud derives the morning prayer from Abraham rising early to stand before God; this interpretive tradition connects the commentary's Abrahamic prayer with its account of the purified person remembering God's name and praying.

column5: Abraham keeps the law and covenant
column6: Sirach remembers Abraham as keeping the law of the Most High and entering covenant; this Jewish praise makes the Abraham-Moses pairing a continuity of divine instruction, not merely shared antiquity.

column5: Moses' blessed memory among later generations
column6: Sirach says Moses is beloved and his memory is blessed; it gives a Jewish witness to the commentary's closing image of Moses' name preserved among those who come later.
The Mishnah plays on the engraved writing of the tablets as freedom for those who study Torah; it turns Moses' written pages into a formative, liberating instruction rather than inert text.

Josephus portrays Abraham challenging inherited polytheism and teaching that one God created the universe; this Jewish retelling gives the commentary's rejection of ancestral custom an explicit monotheistic argument.

column5: old writing announced as fulfilled now
column6: After reading Isaiah, Jesus says the scripture is fulfilled in the hearers' hearing; this Christian interpretation shows how an old page can be presented as a current warning or promise.

column5: tree planted by water remains fruitful
column6: The psalm's watered tree whose leaf does not wither contrasts with the commentary's pasture that dries; its righteous-tree image also gives a counterpart to the surah's successful purified person.
The psalm likens the wicked to chaff driven away, a specific plant-and-wind image that complements the commentary's pasture withering and the rejecter facing loss.

column5: human life like grass and a flower
column6: The psalm says human life flourishes briefly like field grass and then disappears; it makes the commentary's contrast between the temporary worldly life and enduring revelation concrete.
Against the fading human life, the psalm says the Lord's steadfast love is everlasting for those who fear him; this joins the commentary's fear, permanence, and transmission to later generations.

column5: teaching passed to children not yet born
column6: The psalm says the next generation should know the teaching and tell it to their children; this gives a scriptural model for old warning surviving through later hearers.
The psalm asks God to keep the speaker's tears in a bottle and record them in a book; it gives the commentary's divine book of old generations a personal image of what God does not forget.
The psalm says the speaker's days were written in God's book before they came to be; this parallels Moses' statement that the earliest generations are held in a book with God.

column5: names written in the book at the end
column6: Daniel says deliverance comes for those found written in the book; it links a preserved written record to the final fate that the commentary says the first pages describe.

column5: Moses remembered as an unsurpassed prophet
column6: Deuteronomy closes by saying no prophet like Moses arose, whom the Lord knew face to face; it gives a biblical form of the lasting recognition of Moses' name at the end of the surah.
Isaiah commands the testimony to be bound up and instruction sealed among disciples; this gives another image of a warning preserved in writing for a faithful community.
Moses is told to write God's judgment against Amalek in a book and recite it to Joshua; this joins a written record to spoken transmission as the commentary does.

Genesis says Abraham trusted God and was counted righteous; it supplies a specific biblical account of Abraham's response to divine promise behind the commentary's image of him as a model for the successful purified person.

column5: God spoke to ancestors through prophets
column6: Hebrews describes the one God speaking to the ancestors through prophets in many portions and ways; this supports reading the named earlier pages as distinct witnesses within a continuous message.
